reason: The narrative of Genesis 34 does not portray regular people as antagonistic to their leader. The men of Shechem's city listen to and follow Hamor and Shechem's proposal to circumcise themselves; they demonstrate compliance rather than antagonism (וַיִּשְׁמְע֤וּ אֶל־ חֲמוֹר... כָּל־ יֹצְאֵ֖י שַׁ֣עַר עִיר֑וֹ וַיִּמֹּ֙לוּ֙ כָּל־ זָכָֽר). The only conflict present is between Jacob and his sons (Simeon and Levi), where the sons respond defensively to their father's criticism, but this represents family discord rather than the stated relationship of regular people being antagonistic to leadership.
